catalog_quote: [p.116] Both sets of data are sensitive to the same syllable weight hierarchy: CVV > CVC > CV > CVH. This weight hierarchy is manifested in different ways during the two stages of Hupa. In the Sapir data, weight is relevant within a two-syllable window at the left edge of a word, with stress preferentially falling on the initial syllable if the first two syllables are equivalent in weight. In the more recent acoustic data, stress falls on the leftmost CVV syllable and on the root in the absence of any prefixal long vowels. Within the root, stress preferentially falls on the leftmost closed syllable. Syllables closed by a glottal optionally reject stress in any context unless there is no other syllable containing a non-glottal coda. [p.110] Based on the examined data, two factors are relevant for predicting the location of stress in modern Hupa: syllable weight and morphological structure. ... The corpus includes many words containing a single long vocoid, which consistently attracts stress over other syllables regardless of position. [p.112] In words lacking a long vowel, a preference for stressing roots over affixes rears its head. ... In words containing a monosyllabic root and lacking long vowels, stress falls on the root syllable, which is necessarily heavy due to a restriction requiring that roots end in a CVV or CVC syllable.
world_status: statement found in an open source
sweep_summary: Hupa (hupa1239) is not in the catalog. The title search produced two Glottolog items. (1) Leer 1976 'Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan' was located via the ANLA API (item CA965L1976b), downloaded (86-page scan scan, 4.9 MB), scanned at 250 dpi one page at a time, and saved with its scanned and ANLA record; it is a comparative reconstruction of Proto-Athabaskan tone/constriction and vowel-length reflexes in stem syllables, with Hupa appearing only as a column in the correspondence charts, and contains no statement about Hupa word stress (0 scanned hits for stress/accent/pitch): prosody-but-not-word-stress, priority none. (2) Goddard 1928 'Pitch accent in Hupa' (already held by the project, UCPAAE 23:333-338) was re-read in full: a 1904 kymograph study of relative syllable pitch in verb paradigms showing falling pitch in disyllables (peak on the initial prefix), medium-high-low in trisyllabic 1pl forms, and enclitic -te outside the pitch contour; Goddard concludes pitch is not distinctive and mentions stress only as something Hupa hearers correct (p. 338); no placement rule. The best first-hand stress statement read is Gordon & Luna 2004 (BLS 30:105-117, held by the project from the prior search, DOI 10.3765/bls.v30i1.3426): weight hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV > CVH; in Sapir's 1927 texts a left-edge two-syllable window with initial default; in 1995 data stress on the leftmost long vowel, else on the root (usually final), leftmost CVC within polysyllabic roots, optional retraction off glottal-closed syllables; no lexical tone, no reliable secondary stress. Supporting on-disk statements: Golla 1970:40-41 (long vowels most stressed, closed long syllable highest, sentence-initial declination, stress grammatically irrelevant), Woodward 1964:199 as quoted in Gordon & Luna (long syllable stressed, penult default when all short; print-only, low priority), Goddard 1907/1911 (accent on the root in the definite past, on the pre-root syllable in the present). Nothing remains unread that is likely to be a better statement; Woodward 1964 first-hand and Golla 1996 HNAI sketch are the only print-only gaps.

new_statements.citation: Gordon, Matthew & Edmundo Luna. 2004. An intergenerational study of Hupa stress. Proceedings of the Thirtieth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society (BLS 30), 105-117. DOI 10.3765/bls.v30i1.3426.
new_statements.locator: Sec. 5 Conclusions, p. 116 (see also sec. 3.2.1-3.2.3, pp. 110-114; sec. 2.2.4, p. 110 for Sapir-era pattern)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (extracted text of the author PDF) and cross-checked the publisher PDF extracted text pp.1-2 identical text, title 'An Intergenerational Study of Hupa Stress', Gordon & Luna, UCSB, BLS 30 pp.105-117). The quoted passage is at sec. 5 Conclusions, p.116 (the text) and is verbatim; the report's '[..]' elides exactly one sentence ('This weight hierarchy is manifested in different ways during the two stages of Hupa.'). I read secs. 1, 2.2.1-2.2.4, 3.1-3.2.3, 4.1-4.2 and 5 myself: Sapir 1927 texts, 2,230 single-stress words, 91% stressed on one of the first two syllables, initial preferred, weight hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV > CVH deciding within the window (Table 1), no root preference; 1995…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Modern Hupa (1995 speakers, words in isolation): primary stress goes to the leftmost syllable with a long vowel (long vocoid) anywhere in the word; if the word has no long vowel, stress falls on the root syllable (normally word-final/near-final and obligatorily heavy, CVV or CVC); in polysyllabic roots the leftmost CVC wins over CV; a root syllable closed only by h or glottal stop may optionally pass stress to the word-initial syllable. Weight scale CVV > CVC > CV > CVh/CVʔ. In Sapir's 1927 texts the system was instead a left-edge two-syllable window: stress on the heavier of the first two syllables, initial in ties, blind to root/affix status. Acoustic cues: duration, intensity and f0 all mark stress; Hupa has no lexical tone.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'The examined data failed to show convincing evidence for secondary stress' (p.114); in Sapir's texts words with multiple stress marks are too rare for inference (p.106 fn.1).
new_statements.exceptions: CVh/CVʔ root syllables optionally shift stress to the initial syllable (variants, ex. 6); an extra-long vocoid (VV+glide) attracts stress from an earlier long vowel ('door', fn.2); in words with several long vowels the first is most prominent; Sapir-era vs modern difference may reflect narrative vs isolation data or genuine change (sec. 4.1). Golla 1970:40 calls relative stress 'grammatically irrelevant' (non-contrastive) and notes long vowels, esp. in closed syllables, are most stressed and sentence-initial syllables most prominent; Woodward 1964:199 (via G&L) gives long/heavy syllable else penult.
new_statements.domain_note: Modern rule based on words elicited in isolation (citation forms), 2-7 syllables; Sapir-era rule from connected narrative text with Sapir's acute-accent stress marks; Golla 1970's remarks are about the sentence (declination from the first syllables). Stress is non-phonemic/predictable in all accounts.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Hupa proper (Hoopa Valley, natinixwe), not Chilula/Whilkut; Glottolog's language-level node hupa1239 'Hupa-Chilula' covers both. Gordon & Luna's modern data are ~125 isolated words from three Hoopa Valley speakers recorded 1995; their corpus study is Sapir's 1927 Hupa texts (narrators Sam Brown, Emma Frank, Jake Hostler, John Shoemaker).

new_statements.reading: Hupa has weight-sensitive, non-fixed word stress with no lexical tone. In Sapir's 1927 texts stress is confined to a left-edge two-syllable window (initial by default, second syllable when it is heavier; hierarchy CVV > CVC > CV > CVH) and ignores morphology. In 1995 recordings of the last fluent speakers the leftmost long vowel is stressed wherever it stands; failing a long vowel, the (heavy, usually final) root syllable is stressed, with the leftmost CVC in polysyllabic roots and optional leftward retraction off glottal-closed syllables. Cues: duration, f0, intensity; no reliable secondary stress. For catalog purposes: weight-sensitive (quantity) system; left-edge/initial-leaning in the 1927 stage, root/rightward-leaning (typically final) in the modern stage; not a fixed-position language. This file was already held by the project from the prior search and was read in full in this search of works with stress in the title; the two Glottolog title hits (Leer 1976, Goddard 1928) add nothing that supersedes it.

sources.note: Whole paper on stress. Sapir 1927 texts (2,230 words): 91% have stress on one of first two syllables; within that window weight decides (CVV > CVC > CV > CVH), initial preferred in ties, no root preference. Modern (1995) isolated words, acoustic: stress on leftmost CVV (long vocoid); if no long vowel, on the (monosyllabic, heavy) root; within polysyllabic roots leftmost CVC; CVh/CV? syllables optionally pass stress to the initial syllable. Cues: duration, intensity, f0. No convincing secondary stress (p.114).

sources.citation: Golla, Victor K. 1970. Hupa grammar. Ph.D. dissertation, University of California, Berkeley. Section 213/214 'Prosodemes', pp. 39-41.
sources.quote: The relative pitch and stress of the vocalic or voiced segments of a Hupa sentence are grammatically irrelevant and need not be discussed here, except to note that: (1) long vowels are more highly stressed than adjacent short vowels, with the long vowel of a closed syllable most highly stressed. [...] (2) the first syllables of a sentence are more prominent in stress and higher in pitch than those that follow. [...] This regular pattern is interrupted in a number of sentences by a high pitch correlated with heavy stress. This interruption appears to have linguistic significance, and will be treated as a prosodic phoneme, marked /'/
sources.locator: pp. 40-41, section 214.2 'Interjected high pitch' (numbered 213 in the section head)
sources.note: Stress treated as non-phonemic and weight-driven: long vowels outrank short, closed long syllables highest; sentence-initial declination; a 'demonstrative' interjected high-pitch prosodeme is the only phonemic prominence. No fixed positional rule.

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle. 1905. The morphology of the Hupa language. UCPAAE 3. Berkeley: University Press.
sources.note: Scattered remarks only: past vs present definite root differences attributed to 'a sort of accent, which seems to consist mostly in dwelling on the syllable for a longer time' (p.37); 'the always weak stress is on the first syllable throughout the singular' of one paradigm. No general rule.

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle. 1911. Athapascan (Hupa). In F. Boas (ed.), Handbook of American Indian Languages, Part 1 (BAE Bulletin 40), 85-158. Washington: GPO.
sources.quote: The definite present and past differ from each other only in the form and length of the root. The past has the longer and stronger form of the root, if it be variable at all. The accent seems to rest on the root in the past, and on the syllable before the root in the present.
sources.locator: section on definite tenses (scanned excerpt lines 2340-2348 and 3410-3418); cf. Goddard 1907 Phonology of the Hupa Language Part I p. 8 ( line 398): 'The past has a stress accent on the ultima, while the present has the accent on the penult.'
sources.note: Sec. on sounds: past tense 'more strongly accented on the ultima (the root syllable)'; 'The accent seems to rest on the root in the past, and on the syllable before the root in the present' (definite tenses). Morphologically conditioned remarks, no general word-stress rule.

sources.citation: Leer, Jeff. 1976. Spirantization and the development of suprasegmentals in Proto-Athabaskan. Ms. dated 7-21-76, 24 pp. + typescript 30 pp. Alaska Native Language Archive item CA965L1976b (Glottolog ref 167470).
sources.quote: One of the major purposes of this paper is to formulate a hypothesis of the development of tone in modern Athabaskan from an earlier (pre-Proto-Athabaskan) system of vowel nuclei. [...] In the case of Athabaskan, however, the development of tone depended not only on the vowel nucleus, but on the final consonant of the syllable. If the final consonant was glottalized, the reflex of the tone is opposite of what it is if the final consonant was not glottalized.
sources.locator: Typescript pp. 1-2 (pp. 2-3), Chart 4 'Reflexes of Proto-Athabaskan Syllable Types' (p. 20) and notes (p. 21); the handwritten ms. copy follows and duplicates the typescript.
sources.note: Nothing about Hupa word stress. The 'suprasegmentals' are Proto-Athabaskan tone/constriction and vowel-length reflexes in stem syllables; Hupa appears only as a column in the correspondence charts (Chart 4, reflexes of PA syllable types; light/heavy stem forms, p. 20-21 and the passage on the PCA nominalizing suffix leaving heavy stems). The scanned of all 86 pages has zero hits for 'stress' or 'accent' and zero for 'pitch'. Comparative-historical, not a description of Hupa prosody.

sources.citation: Goddard, Pliny Earle. 1928. Pitch accent in Hupa. University of California Publications in American Archaeology and Ethnology 23(6): 333-338.
sources.quote: The simple Hupa verb consists of the stem which is the final syllable, and of the subject pronominal prefixes which are the first syllables. [...] When the dissyllabic forms, of which there are twenty-four examples, are considered, we find either an even or a falling pitch. [...] The first person plural has three syllables. The word begins on a syllable of medium pitch, rises to high, and falls to low. [p. 338:] It does not seem that pitch or pitch change is used to differentiate between words similar in other respects. [...] Hupa hearers correct mispronunciations which are due to ignoring of glottal elements and sometimes to misplaced stress, but do not correct a white speaker in regard to pitch.
sources.note: A 1904 kymograph study (one speaker, Julius Marshall) of relative syllable pitch in verb paradigms. Findings: disyllabic verbs have falling pitch (peak on the initial prefix syllable, average interval about a minor third); trisyllabic 1pl forms are medium-high-low (peak on the second, subject-prefix syllable); with the future enclitic -te the pattern is high-medium-low or high-low-low, the enclitic being 'felt as something added on'; the stem (final syllable) is never the pitch peak. Pitch is judged non-distinctive; stress exists (misplaced stress is corrected by Hupa hearers) but its placeme…
